# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in

194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader

203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser

205

207	```

209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).

214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.

217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full

220	```

225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made

235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

  - three bot-repo publish attempts at the 0.78.1 push died mid-transfer ("the remote end

content.text:
Single step is right, and I over-scaffolded. My thoughts:

The ladder earns its ceremony when intermediate commits capture *decisions* — stages that could each go a different way, worth a scratch title and a checkpoint. This sweep has none of that structure: it's one homogeneous transformation applied 900 times. Batching it by file group creates checkpoints nobody will ever return to, at the cost of per-rung `jj new` / fast-validate / `jj describe` ceremony, and the published history is identical either way (opening + close-out) since the ladder squashes to nothing.

The two things the ladder would nominally buy are both already covered:

- **Undo safety**: jj's op log gives restore points without commits, and the mechanical part (`→`, `…`, `–`) is a rerunnable one-liner — losing it costs seconds.
- **Mid-course review**: the real risk isn't breakage (no test asserts on any of the four characters, and clippy/test catch anything structural) — it's my em-dash judgment being systematically off across 658 sites. But the ready-to-commit gate already handles that: you review the working-copy diff and we iterate before anything commits. If you'd rather sanity-check early, I can pause after the first big file (init.rs, 70 sites) and show you the pattern before grinding through the rest — a conversational checkpoint, no commit needed.

The one discipline worth keeping from the multi-step plan: run `cargo test` once between the mechanical pass and the em-dash pass, so if something does break we know which half did it. That's free.

So: cycle stays two published commits — the 0.78.2-0 opening you're reviewing now, then all sweep work lands in the 0.78.2 close-out. When you give the word I'd adjust the two records that currently promise a ladder (the In Progress plan bullets and the chores-16 intro line) to say single-step, which also slightly simplifies the opening diff. No actions taken yet.

key its description, the command/context it's `used by`, its default (or a value marked `# example`

- the four named characters went to zero: `->` and `...` by mechanical replace, the 708 em
  dashes each given their structural decision (colon for term-elaboration, comma for
  continuation, parentheses for asides, sentence splits for contrasts), converted by four

  gists at cap+1, and the mechanical `...` conversion broke the length test; the function now
  reserves room for the suffix and stays within `max` (contract tightened, test to `<= CAP`)

  output; they render as `-` runs now, and the README's config samples were regenerated from
  the installed binary so the docs match what the code emits
- line width: string literals split with backslash continuation (content byte-identical),
  comments re-wrapped, trailing `// OK:` comments moved above their statement where wrapping
  was awkward; exempt as literal rows: the JSONL fixture strings in the transcript /
  bot-session tests, and comment URLs

Riding in the same commit: the cycle records, the Done-retirement sweep of four
refactor-program entries into done.md, the `0.78.1` ladder-ref backfill, and the first
generic-custom.md-test findings logged in [notes/dogfood.md](../dogfood.md).

### Delegation notes

Four Sonnet agents converted the em-dash batches and a fifth did the line-width pass; two
incidents worth remembering when delegating sweeps:

- one batch agent "corrected" scope creep it thought it saw, reverting 29 already-converted
  arrows back to `→` because it compared against a pre-sweep baseline; caught by the
  post-batch character audit. A delegated sweep needs the invariant stated as "the end state
  is X", not "convert only Y": agents infer baselines
- the line-width agent first placed the continuation break-space after the backslash, which
  Rust strips with the leading whitespace, silently corrupting a fixture string; its own
  `cargo test` run caught it. String splits verify by test, not by eye

You're not mistaken, and the strongest evidence is the stuff we didn't plan for:

- **The sweep found a real bug.** `truncate_chars` was silently over-cap because a banned character was doing arithmetic work nobody remembered. That's the class of thing invisible punctuation does: it hides in contracts.
- **The invariant is now enforceable for one grep.** Before: 863 sites of debt, growing, checkable only by four separate searches that had *twice* been run as subset audits that missed things. After: `grep -P '[^\x00-\x7F]' src/ tests/` returns empty, forever, and any regression is a one-line diff review. Rules you can check mechanically get kept; rules that need judgment audits decay — this cycle is itself the proof, since the audit count was wrong both times it was taken.
- **The user-facing payoff is concrete**: every message vc-x1 prints can now be typed back into a grep by a user chasing it through logs or source, and the output renders identically in any terminal, font, or CI log — box-drawing and typographic characters are exactly what mangles first in hostile environments.

The honest costs, so your confidence is calibrated rather than sold to:

- **~700 conversions were judgment calls made by lesser models.** I audited the flagged sites and the patterns, but a residue of slightly-awkward phrasings almost certainly survives. They're cosmetic, they surface naturally when files get touched, and each is a one-word fix — but the diff is not artisanal throughout.
- **`git blame` on those 65 files now hits this commit first.** One well-titled commit mitigates it (`blame --ignore-rev` handles it entirely), but it's a real archaeology tax.
- **Output text changed**, so anything external that pattern-matched the old separators would break. Nothing we know of does — vc-x1 has never promised machine-parsable output — but it's the one externally visible edge.

The frame I'd actually defend: the alternative wasn't "free." Keeping source non-compliant meant the rule carried a permanent asterisk, and rules with standing exceptions stop being rules. This cycle retired the asterisk and replaced four fuzzy searches with one exact one. That's worth a mechanical afternoon.

message.content: How is elispse character rendered on a terminal and what was the consequence of the bug?

content.text:
Two-part answer, and the second part deserves honest calibration.

**How `…` renders.** U+2026 HORIZONTAL ELLIPSIS is one *character* but its terminal treatment varies:

- In most Western-configured terminals it occupies **one column** — three dots squeezed into a single cell, visually denser than `...`.
- Its Unicode East-Asian-Width class is "ambiguous," so terminals configured for CJK legacy compatibility render it **two columns** wide. Same string, different width, which is exactly the kind of nondeterminism you don't want in column-capped output.
- In a font missing the glyph it renders as tofu (`□`) or a replacement mark.
- Byte-wise it's 3 UTF-8 bytes for 1 displayed cell, so anything reasoning about "length" has three different answers: 3 bytes, 1 char, 1-or-2 columns. `...` is 3 bytes, 3 chars, 3 columns — all three metrics agree.

**What the bug actually was.** Calibrating my earlier "real bug" claim: it was latent and cosmetic, not a correctness failure. `truncate_chars` was documented "truncate to `max` chars" but implemented as *content* to max, then append `…` — so truncated gists in `bot-session` output were 101 characters against an intended 100 cap, and the test had quietly codified the off-by-one (`<= CAP + 1`). Consequences in practice:

- A gist line could exceed the designed cap by one column (or two in an ambiguous-width terminal) — mild wrap/misalignment risk in exactly the tool whose job is tidy columnar transcript display.
- The subtler cost was the invisible-mismatch one: a user copying a truncated gist got a character they couldn't type or grep for, and searching the transcript for `...` would silently not match `…`.

What the sweep did was *surface* it: the mechanical `…`→`...` conversion pushed truncated output to 103 chars, the assertion finally tripped, and the fix made the function honor its own documentation — content plus suffix within `max`, test tightened to `<= CAP`. Net user-visible change: a truncated gist now shows 97 content characters plus `...` in a guaranteed 100 total, instead of 100 plus a floating one-or-two-column tail.

The plain version: the fancy ellipsis is one squeezed-together character whose width on screen depends on the terminal's settings, so lines using it could come out slightly different widths for different users, and it can't be typed or searched for. The old code also let truncated lines run one character past their stated limit, and the test had been written to accept that. Nothing was crashing — it was a tidiness bug in a tidiness feature — and the sweep's conversion is what finally made it visible and fixed.
